item.title: Building Positive Neural Plasticity in the Bright Mind
item.description:
Neuroplasticity

Building Positive Neural Plasticity in the Bright Mind

Mental flexibility allows for innovation and new patterns for greater adaptation.

Posted September 14, 2026

Key points
  • Mental flexibility and neural plasticity go hand in hand and inform how we choose to nurture our mindset.
  • Neural plasticity is the ability of the brain to change based on experience, environment, and memory.
  • When a child is supported and has emotional equanimity, they thrive and knowledge is easily acquired.
  • We can build positive neural plasticity when our mind is open, awareness is present, and intention is clear.

“You are capable of more than you know.” — Glinda (The Wizard of Oz)

Our mind is composed of knowledge (perceptions of the present moment made tangible through our five senses and our autobiographical memories) and energy flow (electrical pulses that fire across neural paths and transfer information).

The way we perceive information is directly related to the attention and intention of how we choose to cultivate our neural pathways. Neural pathway development is similar to Dorothy Gale’s journey on the yellow brick road—unbound, on uncharted territory, and full of possibility.

Navigating the Storms of Neuroadaptation

Life is not always rainbows, sunshine, and happy endings. But when we encounter unexpected showers, we can gain wisdom from walking in the rain. We learn to avoid puddles (unless we are the few who leapfrog puddle to puddle). Or we may choose a path lined with trees to deflect the raindrops.

Building mental flexibility, neural strength, and connections allows for innovation and new patterns for greater adaptation. With enhanced mental flexibility, we can spontaneously discover a new highway leading to a shortcut home, gifted with a moment of insight. Our growth is directly related to our openness that can amplify (or hinder) our neuroadaptation.

The Yin and Yang of Brain Expansion

Neuroindividuality is at our forefront. Each of our brains has its own entire Land of Oz, illuminating distinct yellow brick roads. The minds of our twice-exceptional (2e) adults and children are just that: places where pathways have unexpected detours, backcountry roads, and high-speed interchanges.

The yin and yang of brain expansion is through time and space. Brain development is asynchronous—our brain has the ability to change throughout our life based on attention, intention, and experience.

Mental flexibility and neural plasticity go hand in hand and inform how we choose to nurture our mindset. Parents, educators, and community directly shape and build the roadways in our children’s brains.

Neurons That Fire Together, Wire Together

Neural plasticity is the process of building and strengthening neural patterns in the brain. This is the ability of the brain to change throughout an individual's life based on experience, environment, and memory, known as the Hebbian notion.

Put succinctly: “Neurons that fire together, wire together.”

A common firing pattern creates a circuit and memory that shapes and develops the brain. These pulses across the brain relay information about our perceived environment. The next step is our mindset, or how we choose to pay attention to information in the present moment, encouraging a neural pathway.

The Challenge of Paving New Roads

Can we build neural connections for new skills from scratch? Yes, but it may take more time to develop a completely new neural pathway.

A recent study in Richard Anderson’s laboratory at Caltech has shown that learning a new skill is easier for the brain if a common neural pattern has already developed. The lead authors, Sofia Sakellaridi and Vassilios Christopoulos, used a brain-machine interface paradigm to track learning and individual neuron firing. They found that learning is restricted by pre-existing neural patterns.

When the participant was acquiring a completely new skill, the neural framework was not in place, and adaptation for neuronal firing in learning a new skill was being developed, as compared to skills that build upon or adapt skills already learned. For example, a violinist can learn to play the bass guitar more easily than the drums, because the neural pattern involved with playing a string instrument has already developed.

Having the pavement for the pathway helps when learning a new similar skill. However, when learning a new skill that does not have as well-paved a neural path, it takes time to build the road through repetition and practice of the skill, where attention and intention are paramount.

Emotional Connections and Meaningful Learning

Often, 2e children have a high level of disconnect when learning new skills. Literally, they may have a roadway built for excellent spatial memory, while their peers require months or perhaps even years to develop a similar ability. On the other hand, they may not have the brain infrastructure required for raising their hand and waiting their turn until they are called on.

Somehow, they always speak out of turn. Behavior does not match the attention and intention of the child, and learning the appropriate behavior can be challenging and frustrating. In extreme cases, failing time and time again to learn a new skill can be demoralizing to a child, lowering self-image and esteem if the skill is not taught with compassion and patience.

This is where the connections with family, teachers, and community are key. Pamela Cantor and her colleagues found that emotional connection is the greatest factor helping children to learn. Specifically, when a child is supported and has emotional equanimity at home, in the classroom, and in the community, the child thrives, and knowledge is easily acquired. Children need to feel engaged with material that is meaningful to them, and the bridge can be an emotional connection.

By contrast, Cantor reports that negative reinforcement and trauma hinder learning. When the mind is stressed, we lack the openness needed to obtain the new skill or information. Instead, the mind and body are absorbed in the fight, flight, or freeze responses associated with anxiety. The mind is off-line. As Dorothy says to the Scarecrow, “How can you talk if you haven’t got a brain?”

The Power of the Arts in Brain Integration

Importantly, the environment can support positive neural connections and strengthen development, or it can hinder development. Positive reward for internal states that are related to meaning can allow for a change to positive neural circuits and positive behaviors.

In a striking example, Mariale Hardiman and her team have found that arts instruction enhanced learning and integration of science content and concepts. Instructors in fifth-grade classrooms in Baltimore, Maryland taught environmental science and astronomy along with singing and dancing.

The arts-integrated students retained the scientific information ten weeks later with greater accuracy than students who had studied the same material without arts instruction. Importantly, this demonstrates how learning works across three domains:

  1. Learning novel information becomes meaningful when it activates our senses.
  2. Our brains are wired for retention when there is an emotional connection.
  3. We retain material better because it is integrated into our senses, emotions, and body.

Trust Your Yellow Brick Road

Each of the characters in The Wizard of Oz searched for something outside of themselves, only to discover it had resided within them all along. We can build positive neural plasticity when our mind is open, awareness is present, and our intention is clear.

Trust your neurodiverse yellow brick roads. Take yourself on an adventure, get lost, have fun, and walk joyfully along the glistening path you are on. Each of these is made of gold bricks, the building blocks that enhance the neural plasticity of your mind.

“Experience is the only thing that brings knowledge, and the longer you are on Earth, the more experience you are sure to get.” — The Wonderful Wizard of Oz

item.title: Our Projections, Our Selves
item.description:
Projection

Our Projections, Our Selves

Personal Perspective: What you can learn about yourself in what you think about others.

Posted September 14, 2026

Key points
  • Projections come from parts of ourselves we don't like and attribute to others instead of acknowledging.
  • They're hard to recognize because we believe our perceptions reflect objective reality.
  • A friend or partner's objection to your characterization offers an opportunity to explore your own feelings.
  • Understanding the feelings we project onto others can mean greater self-knowledge and better relationships.

We do it a lot, but we’re not aware of it. Projection is when we perceive a feeling inside of us as coming from the outside, usually from a person close to us. When, for example, we might accuse a lover of flirting instead of recognizing our own roving eye or guilt for past infidelities.

Generally, projections are parts of ourselves we don’t like, our negative or shadow self that we attribute to others in order to maintain our self-regard. The results can be tragic when we project onto groups we think of as “those people” the shameful qualities we don’t want to see in ourselves, such as aggression, dishonesty, or “animal” sexuality.

The trouble, of course, is that blaming others for our own disturbing feelings distorts reality and can erode relationships. But what to do about projection is a challenge. It’s difficult recognize that our assessment of others may not be objective reality, which is why it can be helpful to investigate projections when the opportunity arises.

It did for my husband Peter and I recently when the context was innocuous enough to make them nonthreatening: the care and feeding of our dogs. In what had come to be an ongoing battle, we discovered mutual projections based on even quirkier individual ones. It was a kind of projection sink hole, you might say.

Noticing that my husband was now routinely giving our two dogs, like, 20 treats a day, I insisted he cut back. They were getting fat, I argued, and he was turning them into beggars. He coolly responded that their total caloric intake was the same as ever and offered various calculations. Nonetheless, they’d gained weight and so, with this rare evidence of my ordinarily Mr. Spock-like husband’s utter irrationality, I quickly ratcheted up to “You’re acting crazy!” Although he didn’t just admit it and desist, he did something that might be more helpful in the long run: He pointed out my own pet care madness.

As he reminded me just that morning, when it was way too hot to take the dogs on a nearby hiking trail, I got up at 6 AM to drive half an hour to the beach despite being tired and facing a full workday. Struck by the truth of what he said, I even confessed to being guilt-ridden when I don’t take them to roam free, imagining that I can feel their claustrophobia and depression. Peter was quick to note that freedom is something animals like but don’t need, as I seemed to think. There were plenty of city dogs who got leashed walks twice a day and were happy just to chill at home with their people.

I conceded his point as he did mine, not that either of us have changed our pet care. However, there has been a promising shift.

Calling each other out for craziness is hardly rare in couples—and isn’t necessarily projection. Yet I think for us it was. Talking it over, we realized we both pride ourselves on our rationality and left-brain thinking. Individually, we’ve used that orientation both as a life strategy and as a prop to maintain self-esteem. Much easier to accuse the other of irrationality—no less craziness—than see it in our supposedly rational selves. Having it revealed, however, we were both chastened enough to want to investigate the weird projections that had motivated it.

What we found is that even projection as innocuous as how we treat our pets repays consideration. It’s easy to recognize a feeling as projection when its recipients are those most agreeable of companions who never really insist on the treats or hikes that we so anxiously offer them. Calming those anxieties, though, is the hard part. For that, we tried psychoanalytic thinking—that is, looking into our motives and their origins.

As I thought about what I believed to be my dogs’ urgent need to roam free, I remembered the urgency I felt about “breaking out” of a childhood home filled with sadness and secrets, as if it had imprisoned me. My resources were limited but since nothing had stopped me from freely exploring the world, really, I soon realized it must have been my own unacknowledged fear of leaving the only life I knew.

Although I have lived a radically different life from the one I grew up with, I think I was never convinced that I could manage it. Some part of me has been stuck in the fear that my courage would fail and I would find myself back there, which has led me to forever replay my “breakout.” And now to project it onto my dogs, who hardly object.

On reflection, Peter discovered that he felt so bad when our 13-year-old dog Tallulah fell ill and soon after took second place to our lively pup, Olive, that he started to “comfort Tallulah” with treats (which he couldn’t deny Olive either). In his childhood, he said, there were no comforting hugs, no soothing words, no special outings. His depressed mother comforted herself with food, despite her diabetes, and Peter followed suit. Now he was doing it with our dogs.

Neither of our projections onto our pets have abated as quickly as our mutual accusations of craziness, but awareness is a beginning. Peter can no longer dole out Pup-Peroni without knowing why he’s doing it, nor can I scramble awake at dawn to take the pooches for a hike without thinking about my own insecurities. Hopefully, as we track our weird projections, we’ll settle into a reality that doesn’t require them.

item.title: Why Do I Get Anxious Before a Doctor’s Appointment?
item.description:
Chronic Illness

Why Do I Get Anxious Before a Doctor’s Appointment?

Six reasons why pre-appointment anxiety makes sense when you have chronic illness.

Posted September 14, 2026

Key points
  • Medical appointment anxiety is a normal part of living with chronic illness.
  • Anxiety can be an adaptive, sensible response to real medical risk factors.
  • Some people develop medical PTSD from past experiences, which contributes to pre-appointment anxiety.
  • To manage the anxiety, set aside time before and after appointments to offer yourself compassion.
The Faint, Pietro Longhi, c. 1744
Source: "The Faint" by Pietro Longhi / CC0 1.0 Universal Public Domain Dedication

I wish it were only the fluorescent lighting and the uncomfortable intimacy of sharing private physical details with a virtual stranger that made medical appointments anxiety-provoking. But unfortunately, when living with chronic illness, there are a bunch of other factors that create medical appointment anxiety.

Many individuals with chronic illness recognize the tension and uncertainty that show up before an appointment. Some of us even understand that it makes sense to feel anxious given systemic barriers, past experiences, and the fragile balance of hopeful-but-not-too-hopeful expectations. And yet, I repeatedly see clients be incredibly hard on themselves for feeling anxious before appointments.

So here’s a clear case for why you might feel medical appointment anxiety, just in case you needed to hear it.

6 Reasons for Medical Appointment Anxiety

  1. Concern about test results or needing another procedure. Receiving scary test results or knowing an appointment could lead to another painful procedure is behind a lot of medical appointment anxiety. From this perspective, it makes sense to fear the worst. It’s unfair to expect yourself to be perfectly steady while receiving information about your own body not working the way it’s “supposed” to. Anxiety is an adaptive response.
  2. Fear of being misunderstood or not believed. Sometimes we anticipate the pain of not being believed to try to get ahead of our suffering. If we expect we won’t be believed, maybe it won’t sting as much. And even deeper, this fear is often fueled by the uncomfortable thought: What if the doctor believes that I’m exaggerating or making up my symptoms?
  3. Anxiety around remembering/forgetting details. The cognitive load before medical appointments is high, especially when you’re seeing a new provider. There’s pressure to remember everything you meant to say so that you can advocate for yourself and get the care you need. At the same time, doctors may ask highly specific details about your symptoms. When did it start? How often? On a scale of 1–10? There can be anxiety around whether you’ll know the “right” answers about your own body, and whether missing something will cost you the care you need.
  4. Buildup increases tension. Some specialists have waitlists that are over a year long. When we are waiting for something so meaningful—like an appointment that could allow us to feel better—the anticipation can create an environment of anxiety. The longer the buildup, the more space anxiety has to expand, often only releasing once the event has passed.
  5. Concern about financial, energy, and time costs. Going to appointments is a big undertaking. Between time off from work, transportation to the appointment, and uncertainty around finances, there are a lot of moving pieces involved in a medical appointment that could go “wrong.” When you recognize that, some anxiety is to be expected.
  6. Carrying previous experiences with you. Previous negative experiences with medical professionals can prime the body with anxiety before an appointment. Some individuals even develop medical PTSD, which is a set of trauma responses tied to medical experiences that interfere with daily life. When an individual experiences medical PTSD or medical trauma, the body sometimes anticipates danger in situations that may not be dangerous now, but were in fact dangerous in the past. That anticipation creates hypervigilance (that feeling of being on high alert) and anxiety in the body.

What Can You Do?

The next time you’re feeling intense anxiety leading up to a doctor’s appointment, try identifying which of the six reasons above (there can be multiple) is motivating your anxiety. Then, the most powerful thing you can do to help yourself is to remind yourself that your anxiety makes sense. Offer yourself some validation and compassion.

I also recommend setting aside time before and after the appointment to comfort yourself and release tension. Even just five minutes where you sit down, talk with yourself kindly and compassionately about the anxiety, and say something like: I can feel this. I can do this. I trust myself. I am safe.

item.title: What Happens to Siblings When Parents Age
item.description:
Family Dynamics

What Happens to Siblings When Parents Age

Caregiving can strain family bonds—or become an opportunity to repair them.

Posted September 14, 2026

Key points
  • Old family roles and unresolved resentments often resurface when a parent needs more care.
  • Unequal caregiving can leave one sibling overwhelmed and another criticized or shut out.
  • Conflict over money, housing, or medical care may reflect deeper wounds that began years earlier.
  • Clear communication, shared responsibility, and forgiveness can strengthen the whole family.

This post is Part 3 of a series.

I’ll never forget the day my sister put my mom on an airplane, looked me in the eyes, smiled, tapped me on the shoulder and said, “You’re it!”

For years, she had taken increasingly greater care of our aging mother—checking in every day, taking her to doctors’ appointments, and being there for her in a thousand other ways. When Mom eventually moved to California, my sister passed the caregiving baton to me.

While there were unspeakably difficult challenges during the years leading up to Mom’s passing, taking primary responsibility for her care turned out to be one of the greatest joys of my life. Sharing responsibility for our mother’s happiness, health, and well-being as she grew older was the right thing to do. It also left my older sister and younger brother deeply grateful.

Sibling relationships can be complicated, and they can either help or hinder families as parents grow older. There’s no such thing as a perfect sibling relationship. But brothers and sisters who get caught in corrosive rivalries and long-held resentments can suffer immeasurably. Those who are blessed with closeness—or are willing to work toward it—can benefit immeasurably.

The same dynamics can apply to only children, whose stepbrothers, stepsisters, cousins, or close friends become sibling-like members of the family caregiving circle.

When sibling relationships are riddled with animosity, grudges, distrust and festering resentment, everyone in the family can be affected. On the other hand, brothers and sisters who communicate openly, earn and strengthen one another’s trust, support each other, share responsibility for their aging parents, and find ways to work through their differences can create a powerful source of stability for the entire family.

As aging parents face new challenges, unwelcome changes, and losses, some brothers and sisters put in the time and effort to work things out. And, as family therapists and family business consultants across the world—including yours truly—will tell you, some don’t.

Figuring out how to cooperatively deal with difficult decisions and painful realities isn’t easy. Old family roles have a way of resurfacing. One sibling may feel they’re doing everything. Another may feel criticized or left out. Someone may believe Mom or Dad has always favored one child over another. Decisions about medical care, money, housing, and end-of-life wishes can quickly become about much more than the decision at hand.

When siblings battle endlessly in family war zones, aging parents can become caught in the crossfire. Already dealing with difficult changes and challenges, they may also find themselves carrying sadness, frustration, and divided loyalties between the children they love.

But change is possible.

Siblings who have been unwilling or unable to heal their relationships sometimes soften as Mom or Dad grows older, becomes ill, or dies. A family crisis can remind us of what really matters. A brother or sister may come to the aid of a grieving parent who has just lost a partner. Long-held resentments and judgments may begin to lose their grip. Someone may become willing to forgive, apologize, or seek professional help.

Even when it seems impossible to let go of old pain and make peace, there are things we can do to strengthen our sibling and family relationships.

You may be drawn to this possibility in the rawness of sorrow, the joy of a family celebration, or simply in a rare moment when something inside you says, "Enough. I want things to be better."

Making peace with a sibling will not only benefit your parents. It may free your own heart of a heaviness, open new doors of possibility, and set a precedent for how disagreements and hurts are handled in your family for generations to come.

Here are a few steps that can help:

1. Take a breath and take stock. Give yourself credit for being willing to look honestly at what is happening in your family, rather than simply reacting to it.

2. Talk it through with someone you trust. A close friend, family member, therapist, clergy member, or other trusted confidant can help you sort through what is weighing most heavily on your heart. Be willing to tell the truth about how you feel.

3. Get clear about what needs to change. Ask yourself what a reasonably good outcome would look like—not only for you, but for your sibling, your parents, and the rest of the family.

4. Set a goal. Think about what would allow your heart to be more at peace. Make a promise to yourself to do what you reasonably can to move the relationship in that direction.

5. Consider your options patiently. Explore the steps you could take to create a kinder, more collaborative relationship. You don’t have to solve everything at once.

6. Create a game plan. Write down what you hope to accomplish and how you might approach the conversation. Give yourself time to think it through, and consider asking a trusted person for constructive feedback.

7. Take the first step. Explain calmly what you would like to accomplish. Make a humble request for a conversation. Express gratitude where it’s genuine. And, when appropriate, be willing to apologize for your part in what has gone wrong.

8. Be patient with the process. Take one small step at a time. Slow down when old triggers and disagreements surface. Stay focused on what you’re trying to build rather than winning an old argument.

9. Notice and acknowledge progress. As things improve—even in small ways—voice your appreciation and share the credit. Let your parents and other family members experience the benefits of a stronger sibling bond without putting them in the middle.

10. Give yourself credit for choosing a better way forward. Becoming a better version of yourself can help create a better version of your family.

We cannot rewrite our childhoods or erase every hurt between brothers and sisters. Nor can we force a sibling to change. What we can do is decide how we want to show up now.

As our parents move through the later chapters of their lives, the ways we treat one another matter. We can add to the fear, tension, and uncertainty they are already facing—or we can become allies in creating greater peace, stability, and love around them.

Sometimes one person deciding to take that first step is where a family begins to change.

To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

-----------------------------------------------------
Author’s Note: This post is adapted from my book, Raising an Aging Parent: Conversations for the Second Half of Life. It is the third installment in a three-part series exploring the changing dynamics of aging families. Part 1 explored Caring for an Aging Parent. Part 2 was about What Aging Parents Want Their Adult Children to Understand.

item.title: Why Mudita Is a Therapist's Superpower
item.description:
Jealousy

Why Mudita Is a Therapist's Superpower

Envy and jealousy undermine authentic happiness.

Posted September 14, 2026

Key points
  • For more than two thousand years Buddhist psychology has offered antidotes to the mind's malaise.
  • Psychotherapy allows patients—even if just for 55 minutes—to feel good-enough.
  • Consumer-based capitalist societies depend on the human compulsion to desire more-different-better.

During my second graduate program I had the privilege of studying with Robert Thurman, who taught me the Buddhist concept of mudita. If you didn't already know, Professor Thurman, who recently passed, spent much of his scholarly life translating Tibetan Buddhist thought for Western audiences. He presented to our class the concept of mudita as one of the four immeasurables of Buddhist psychology alongside loving-kindness, compassion, and equanimity. Professor Thurman explained that mudita is genuine, embodied joy at another person's joy—taking real pleasure in another person's pleasure.

To understand mudita, it's best to start by thinking of its opposite, our use of the German word "Schadenfreude," which means taking pleasure in another person's suffering. I believe "compersion" is the closest English gets to the opposite of Schadenfreude, but the word has been co-opted by the polyamorous community and is most commonly used to mean taking pleasure in witnessing your lover be satisfied by another lover. Thus, as psychotherapists we may wish to steer clear of compersion. English does not have another term for taking unadulterated pleasure in another person's pleasure or success, so I use mudita.

Here is why mudita might be our clinical superpower: Consumer-based capitalist societies exploit the human compulsion to desire more-different-better. Nothing is ever "good-enough" for long—when we become vice president we start eyeing the presidency, when we buy a three bedroom house we imagine our next house with a pool, when we fly first-class we start eyeing private. Capitalism is driven by the thought "I'll be happy when I attain [the next better thing]," and there's always a next—premium, first class, upper class, gold card, platinum card, black card. We are all clawing our way up ladders of subtle elitism whenever we shop for anything.

I used the word "unadulterated" above because subconsciously there is often jealousy or envy when people hear about the success of others; again, this is the motor that drives our society—the propensity to continuously want more-better-different, to be satisfied only briefly. We are all aware that our minds function analogously to hedonic treadmills; once a desire is sated it is soon replaced by another desire.

In addition, many people subconsciously and consciously perceive the world as a zero-sum game, a finite pie that means if someone else takes a slice then there's one less for them. We're all familiar with hoarding and the growing disparity of resources allocated to a minority of humans while others suffer.

I would be remiss if I didn't mention the subconscious effects of social media and why it's so entrancing for people who desire more-better-different. TikTok and Instagram obviously supply an infinite flow of more-better-different things and experiences for our minds to desire. Our minds watch beautiful, glitzy, smiling people, and assume (incorrectly) that they are happy, then yearn to attain (buy) whatever these people are wearing or doing, assuming (again incorrectly) that it is what they are wearing or doing that is causing any putative happiness. And obviously legacy advertising also equates self-worth and happiness with acquisition and attainment of this elusive more-better-different so this is not a recent phenomenon.

Under these tacit societal arrangements, most people harbor clandestine, frequently disavowed jealousy toward the successes of friends, colleagues, and even strangers encountered IRL and online, an envy rarely spoken because it is culturally unacceptable to admit, and seldom examined because examining it would require confronting the absurd subconscious assumptions mentioned above.

Meanwhile Buddhist psychology has offered antidotes to the mind's malaise for over two thousand years. Leading psychotherapists understand how the mind operates and know that authentic happiness depends on being able to be genuinely happy for other people. This is one of the reasons why giving causes greater happiness than hoarding.

Our unadulterated happiness for our patients' wins is different from the tinge of jealousy and envy our patients may feel from their friends and acquaintances and even loved ones. Thus, mudita is our superpower. We know that our own happiness depends on our ability to forego envy and jealousy and thus we rejoice wholly and authentically with our patients about their successes… allowing them—even if just for 55 minutes—to feel good-enough.

item.title: Which Young Adults Enjoy Good Sex?
item.description:
Sex

Which Young Adults Enjoy Good Sex?

A study shows that one newly identified indicator makes a significant difference.

Posted September 14, 2026

Key points
  • Researchers have identified many factors that contribute to young lovers' sexual satisfaction.
  • A recent study has found a new one—comprehensive sex education years earlier in high school.
  • Meanwhile, many studies show that high-school sex education has no impact on teen pregnancy rates.

For decades, psychologists and sexuality professionals have pondered this question: How can young adults enjoy mutually satisfying lovemaking? In dozens of studies, they’ve identified many factors that contribute to satisfying young-adult sex:

  • Young adults’ individual psychological makeup
  • Their relationships with their parents, families, and friends
  • Their parents’ willingness to discuss sex, or refusal to mention it
  • Their experience, if any, of sexual trauma: child sex abuse, sexual coercion, and sexual assault
  • The quality of sexual communication and assertiveness in the relationships they develop
  • Their exposure to pornography

All these factors play some role in young adults’ sexual satisfaction. But they don’t entirely explain it. A recent study has added a new element to the list, one never previously considered—the type of sex education young adults received, or did not receive, in high school.

The Study

For a study published in the peer-reviewed Journal of Sexual Medicine, a Ph.D. sex therapist affiliated with a large sex therapy practice in Chicago surveyed 224 coupled young adults about their lives, their relationships, and the quality of their partner sex. But unlike previous studies, this one included questions about the sex education they’d received in high school, if any—whether they’d been taught what social conservatives advocate, abstinence until marriage, or what social liberals promote, comprehensive sex ed, instruction about all contraceptive methods, with emphasis on routine use of condoms during intercourse to avoid sexually transmitted infections (STIs).

Independent of all the variables previously mentioned, the young adults most likely to report enjoyable partner sex said their high schools had provided comprehensive sex education. The researcher called her study “the first of its kind,” and concluded that it provides “convincing evidence” that years after high school, young people’s exposure to comprehensive sex education enhanced their sexual and relationship satisfaction.

I must say I was surprised to read this study’s result. Back in the 1970s, I worked in family planning and, as a consultant, taught comprehensive sex education in many high school classes. It looked to me like few, if any, of the students paid much attention. But maybe they did….

Teen Pregnancies Have Plummeted: Who Deserves Credit?

The study’s support for what social liberals advocate adds another dimension to the decades-long controversy over public school sex education. The subject became fraught in the 1970s and 1980s, as U.S. teen pregnancies soared, derailing the young mothers’ lives and often relegating their children to poverty and privation. Across the political spectrum, people screamed at government, Do something!

A good deal of research showed that parents were reluctant to discuss sex with their children, so public health advocates pushed high schools to teach pregnancy prevention. But how? Social conservatives lobbied hard for abstinence only, while social liberals touted the comprehensive approach. Republican-led states usually adopted the conservative program; Democratic-led states usually adopted the liberal.

Something worked. According to the Centers for Disease Control (CDC), since 1991, among young women age 15 to 19, pregnancies have declined a whopping 78 percent. The CDC says “the reasons are not clear.” But both conservatives and liberals were quick to claim credit.

The conservatives were mistaken. Many studies have shown that teaching abstinence doesn’t work:

  • Abstinence-only is most deeply entrenched in the South. It’s less popular elsewhere. Figures from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) show that the teen birth rate is highest in the South.
  • Many abstinence-only programs ask teens to sign pledges swearing to remain virgins until marriage. But a CDC study shows that only 12 percent of those who take virginity vows keep them—a failure rate of 88 percent.
  • Researchers at McMaster University in Hamilton, Ontario, analyzed 26 studies of school-based pregnancy-prevention efforts. With abstinence-only, rates often increased.

However, the research shows that comprehensive sex education doesn't fare better:

  • British researchers analyzed eight studies of comprehensive school-based pregnancy- and STI-prevention programs involving 55,157 teens. Before-and-after statistics showed no reductions in pregnancies or STIs.
  • The just-mentioned McMaster University analysis of 26 studies included many comprehensive programs. They had zero impact on teens: no delay of first intercourse, no increased use of contraceptives, and no fewer pregnancies or STIs.

It’s easy to see why abstinence-only doesn’t work. Teens have raging hormones. In the U.S., the average age at first intercourse is 16. By the time they’ve graduated high school, a majority of teens are no longer virgins. Telling them "don’t" is like whispering into a hurricane.

But why doesn’t “comprehensive” sex education work? Because it isn’t comprehensive. It focuses only on contraceptives and STI prevention. It never mentions erotic pleasure or how to negotiate sexual repertoire and frequency. It’s not sex education, but dangers-of-sex education. It tells kids to fasten their seat belts, but doesn’t teach a thing about how to drive.

Happier Sex Years After High School

This brings us back to the study. It shows that while comprehensive sex education doesn’t do what it was developed to accomplish—reduce teen pregnancies and STIs—it has provided one clear benefit: happier lovers years after they graduate high school.

Why? The author does not speculate. Here’s my view as someone who taught comprehensive sex education. As young people’s exposure to any sex information increases, so does their feeling that sex is suitable for discussion. They might not have paid much attention in sex ed class in high school, but the study suggests that it opened their minds to receiving more sex information years later and discussing it with their partners. Such conversations are foundational to sexual happiness.

I wish high school sex education classes focused more on pleasure and actual lovemaking, but that does not appear politically feasible, even in the most politically liberal states. Still, the study shows that despite its shortcomings, lessons about contraceptives and infection prevention eventually increase young adults’ enjoyment of sex. That’s something to celebrate—and a good reason for high schools to continue teaching about contraceptives and sexual infection prevention.

item.title: When People-Pleasing Makes You Less Likable
item.description:
Agreeableness

When People-Pleasing Makes You Less Likable

The surprising relationship between agreeableness and relationship satisfaction.

Posted September 14, 2026

Key points
  • Very high agreeableness can make you seem less confident and trustworthy, not more likable.
  • People-pleasing is usually driven by fear of conflict, not an absence of opinions.
  • Small, honest expressions of preference build more real connection than constant accommodation.

Have you ever worked hard to be easy to get along with, only to discover that other people don't necessarily experience you that way?

Maybe you rarely disagree, typically say yes when someone asks for help, and adjust your plans when someone else has a preference. You think you're being nice. But over time, other people may have trouble figuring out what you actually think, want, or feel.

This is one of the paradoxes of people-pleasing. The behaviors we use to make relationships go smoothly can eventually make it harder for other people to know us. When taken too far, one of our most socially desirable personality traits can start working against us.

What Agreeableness Actually Measures

Agreeableness is one of the five traits in the Big Five framework, the most widely used model of personality in psychological science. People who are high in agreeableness tend to be cooperative, trusting, and warm. These qualities are a genuine social asset, and it's no surprise that research consistently links agreeableness to greater relationship satisfaction.

But is there a point at which accommodating others becomes submission, or when agreeing with or praising someone becomes ingratiating?

Too Much of a Good Thing

When you respond "sounds good" to any proposal, your approval no longer feels meaningful or earned. Similarly, if you always offer praise without any constructive feedback, your compliments start to lose their value.

People who never push back are viewed as less confident and less authentic than people who occasionally express a genuine preference or disagreement. It's hard to get to know someone when they never share their preferences, from choosing the restaurant for dinner to sharing that something you did upset them. Taking it a step further, conflict can actually drive closeness because you find out the relationship can survive honesty, which is the foundation for trust.

People-pleasing tends to backfire in professional settings too. Studies on workplace relationships find that very high agreeableness predicts lower perceived effectiveness as a leader, even among people who are well-liked by their colleagues.

What Drives People-Pleasing?

Think about what you were praised for as a kid. Being the easy one. Remembering everyone's birthday. Going along without making a fuss. That kind of praise feels good, and over time accommodating others becomes part of your identity.

At the same time, when you considered pushing back or sharing a real opinion, you probably felt anxious. You probably worried what would happen if you said the wrong thing. Deciding to stay quiet leads to relief from that uncertainty.

Through positive (e.g., a reward like praise following an accommodating action) and negative (e.g., relief from uncomfortable anxiety when you choose to stay quiet) reinforcement, you can get stuck in a people-pleasing loop.

How to Adjust the Volume on Agreeableness

Personality traits, including agreeableness, shift meaningfully as we age, and making deliberate changes to how we think and behave can shape the direction of that evolution.

For example, people-pleasers often hold the perspective that honesty is risky and that expressing a preference will cost them something. But most people-pleasers have never really tested that belief.

That's where behavioral experiments come in. Each time you express an honest preference in a low-stakes situation and nothing bad happens, you're collecting data. Over time, you will accumulate evidence that pushing back doesn’t lead to dire consequences, making it easier to do so in the future.

So order what you actually want at dinner. Offer your real opinion when someone asks which movie to watch. Say you'd rather meet on Thursday when Tuesday doesn't work. See what happens.

The Bottom Line

People-pleasing usually starts from a good place. The problem isn't the impulse to be kind; it's what happens when accommodation becomes so automatic that you lose yourself.

item.title: The “Children Are Sponges” Idea Is Harmful to Kids
item.description:
Child Development

The “Children Are Sponges” Idea Is Harmful to Kids

Parents and educators are misled into making kids passive.

Posted September 14, 2026

Key points
  • The kids = sponges myth is common but harmful to kids.
  • The myth discourages kids from talking and being active.
  • The myth hides the harms of media for children.
  • The myth is so entrenched in education that it is difficult to dislodge it even though we know it's wrong.

Do you know about baby sea squirts? These little marine creatures begin life actively swimming around, searching the ocean floor for a good home. When they find their spot, each sea squirt glues itself down and never moves again. Because it no longer needs to be active, it doesn’t need its brain anymore, so it eats it.

These sea squirts have found their forever home on some coral but have lost their brains in the process.
Source: Kevin Mc Loughlin / Pixabay

Even though mature sea squirts are brainless, they can teach us a big lesson: Brain health requires being active. This lesson is especially relevant for parents and educators, because there are a lot of forces these days that keep kids passive. Media messages don't help. The internet has over 26 million websites comparing babies and young children to another sedentary marine organism: sponges. Psychologists, pediatricians, and educators are using the kids = sponges comparison to convey that kids are rapid learners who soak up information. That’s true, but the sponge metaphor is a terrible way to get that message across. It implies that babies and children are passive, just absorbing up what goes on around them, like sponges. That idea is not only wrong; it’s harmful.

How the Sponge Message Hurts Kids

Babies and children are naturally active learners, meaning they learn by experimenting, playing, interacting with others. When babies drop a spoon off the highchair, they learn about gravity. When toddlers stack blocks, they learn about objects and how they fit together, and then more about gravity when the blocks fall. These kinds of experiments are key to kids’ brain development and learning about the world. All that active learning grinds to a halt when children are encouraged to be passive sponges. Here are four ways that the kid = sponge myth harms kids:

1. The sponge myth discourages the child's own talking and active learning

Pediatricians use the sponge myth to talk about the importance of talking to children. This message directs parents to pour lots of language on their young sponges, but it hides the importance of children's own talking. Talking is a form of active learning, and the amount that young children engage in conversations promotes their brain development, attention, memory, and readiness for school. Parents who just talk at their kids or talk for their kids aren’t allowing them to have the brain benefits of talking for themselves.

2. The sponge myth misleads parents about the harms of children’s media

With its focus on talking to kids, the sponge myth implies that kid media should be good for children, because kids can just soak up language input from the video. That's wrong; screens create harmful “technoference” that's a barrier to learning, because when kids are watching a screen, they're not talking and they're not being active. The amount of time that children stare at screens is linked to less brain development, poor sleep, obesity, and more. That’s why, contrary to the sponge myth, pediatricians recommend complete abstinence or very little media exposure for infants young children.

3. The kid = sponge idea stunts kids’ emotional development

Distracting a crying child with a video induces more technoference, preventing the child from practicing their own emotion regulation skills. Children who are frequently given tablets as toddlers show more outbursts of frustration and anger when they enter preschool. And for older kids, preventing them from doing their own talking and problem solving short-circuits opportunities to practice social and emotional skills, impairing their independence and launch into adulthood.

4. Educators' embrace of the sponge myth limits children’s practice and active learning in school

Playtime boosts young children’s cognitive, motor, and social development, but now there is less playtime in school, replaced by more sitting still and absorbing information in class, like a sponge. Educators often create a false dichotomy between instruction vs. playtime and think that playtime just takes time away from learning. Instead, children who get more recess are more attentive and have better grades. And playful learning integrates play and active learning for young children.

In older children, active learning leads to faster and deeper learning and reduces achievement gaps, compared to standard high school and college classes in which students are told to absorb information from lectures. Unfortunately, the sponge myth is so entrenched in education that even though active learning is proven to increase learning in school, active learning reforms face significant pushback from educators, parents, and even students themselves.

Inactive kids are not going to eat their brains like sea squirts do, but they are at risk for less learning, brain development, independence, and emotional maturity. We need to move away from thinking about ways to make kids passive and instead let them be the active learners they are born to be. We need to toss out the sponge myth!

item.title: Concede Up: The Power of Correcting in Real Time
item.description:
Resilience

Concede Up: The Power of Correcting in Real Time

Being wrong is human. Doubling down to save face is a choice.

Posted September 14, 2026

Key points
  • Resilient thought can survive discovering that it was wrong.
  • Discernment must be able to turn on itself, testing and revising the conclusions it has already made.
  • Fear and shame can magnify a small error into a consequential failure.
  • Conceding a position when the evidence changes is better thinking, not weakness.

Fall down seven, get back up eight. “I can’t go on. I’ll go on.” Just do it. Stay the course. For God’s sake, keep going. Wagons, ho! There is something ruggedly American and individualistic about relentless persistence. It's better than capitulation, I suppose.

Angela Duckworth’s 2016 book Grit offers a far more nuanced investigation of persistence. It is more than just getting back on the horse and moving forward. Changing course can serve a larger commitment rather than betray it. Still, the life-is-war metaphor remains. Holding one’s ground is strong. Conceding ground is weak.

Most of life, though, is not lived at the mission-critical edge of catastrophe or conquest. We engage in the performance of everyday life. We deal with what is happening and what to do next. Yet, lax habits of mind around nominal stakes can creep into disastrous circumstances. We need to improve our perceptual literacy. That literacy is part of the practice of discernment.

I want to linger over the capacity to adjust. What allows us to catch a read that has gone wrong while we are still living inside it? To earn its name, discernment requires a mechanism for self-correction. Finding out sooner that we’re wrong, and staying wrong less, is a resilience of thought. Finding out we’re not quite right can knock us off balance. What we do next determines whether the error gets corrected or defended.

Being wrong is too frequent a thing to think of as anomalous. Discernment requires an internal governance system that holds us accountable to what we think we know — a fault-detection system. We need to be able to check the read and correct as quickly as possible. The ego needs to be able to overcome its desire to double down. We need to concede up.

In hindsight, we might say, "I would have done X. Now that I see more clearly, it’s obvious." Good on ya. But things often look identical in real time. We assure ourselves, "I know how to tell the difference." Good impulse, but dangerous.

Think of batting average. It’s difficult to hit a curveball. We get fooled. But we expect that will happen, so we adjust. The aim isn’t infallibility; it's to become less wrong over time. Our average improves. Life’s plate appearances are vast. We show up again. We take our cuts.

The Monarch and the Viceroy

Can you discern the difference? The monarch is on the left; viceroy is on the right.
Source: Photos by Jim Hudgins/USFWS and William Powell/USFWS, Public Domain

The prevailing explanation held that the viceroy developed similar coloring to trick predators into thinking it was as distasteful as the beautiful-to-look-at, but nasty-to-taste monarch. The monarch was the real thing. The viceroy was the fake, with second-class status baked right into its name.

In 1991, biologists produced evidence that changed the story. Viceroys were distasteful too. That’s science doing what science does.

It may seem trivial to discover that another butterfly tastes bad, but God dwells in the details. Making finer distinctions may not matter in any one case, but each one makes future distinctions more possible. Monarch and viceroy were always recognized as different butterflies. We misread what the distinction meant.

Sometimes what fools us is our confidence that we understand the difference we noticed. This is where discernment needs to turn on itself; a kind of quality control for the read. Perceptual literacy is recursive and cumulative. Every moment of sharpened attention sharpens future attention.

The Switch

That mechanism must be actively triggered. Ask: "What would have to happen to make me change my mind? And, if it happened, would I?" That’s the switch. Research suggests we can consciously cultivate what scientists call a counterfactual mindset. In experiments published in 2024, prompting people to imagine alternative possibilities made them measurably more receptive to evidence challenging their baseline beliefs. They actively sought out disconfirming data. So, complicate your own suppositions. You don’t have to completely reverse yourself to correct yourself.

Part of why we fail to activate fault detection is shame. We think, "I got it wrong. I should have realized." The embarrassment of being wrong becomes the precise reason we remain wrong. We have the shame backwards.

Being wrong is the human baseline. Knowing you’re wrong and refusing to tell the truth about it is something else. We should be ashamed to know better and double down anyway. A position is not the self. I can think again. Resilient thought can survive discovering that it was wrong.

Double down on a false read long enough and there is a price to pay, in calamity or credibility. It’s time to dispense with a culture that equates changing a position with weakness, flip-flopping, or fence-sitting. We should hold strong principles, yes, and chief among them should be staying flexible enough to self-correct.

Concede up.

To concede is to give up a position. To concede up is to give it up for a better one. I cut my ballast from that position so I may rise.

Take the Note

Nearly every serious practice operates this way. Scientists revise models. Athletes review film. Musicians rehearse. Correction isn’t outside the work. It is the work. Actors have a phrase for this: take the note. A director offers an adjustment. The actor doesn’t explain or defend the first choice. Taking the note does not mean throwing out the whole interpretation. Just serve the play. Put it on its feet, and try again.

My work in performance studies led me to Louis Sass’s Madness and Modernism (1992). Sass traces affinities between schizophrenia and modernist and postmodernist art, especially fragmentation, estrangement, and heightened self-consciousness. Hamlet predates these movements by centuries, but the titular character's “antic disposition” leaves us unsure where performance ends and genuine disturbance begins.

Hamlet turns theatre into a diagnostic tool. In The Mousetrap, a play inside the play, Claudius’s physical response to the reenactment of King Hamlet’s murder becomes evidence. Prince Hamlet uses performance to test whether he has read Claudius correctly.

Here, discernment doesn’t merely make distinctions. It audits the distinctions it has already made. When the read fails, it demands a finer-grained attribution. What exactly did I get wrong? What still holds?

Sometimes resilience means getting back on the horse. Sometimes it means realizing you are riding in the wrong direction before all hope of finding your way back is lost. We will get things wrong. That isn’t the design flaw. The design flaw is refusing to run the diagnostic tool that lets us find out.

Imagine a casual argument. Someone states something incorrect, catches themselves mid-sentence, and pivots. “Wait. No. That’s not right. Let me correct that.” That moment should be applauded, not as a heroic act, but as the foundational requirement of productive human interaction.

Most conversations shouldn’t be wars of attrition where two people defend positions until one surrenders. They should be coalescent efforts to find the shape of what is true. We should ask ourselves: "How quickly can I detect the fault? How precisely can I locate it? How quickly can I revise?"

Get unstuck and stay wrong less. Don’t be ashamed to correct the read. It’s just the truth.

item.title: Pretty Privilege and the Body Positivity Myth
item.description:
Beauty

Pretty Privilege and the Body Positivity Myth

Does being pretty bestow privilege or trap girls in a myth?

Posted September 14, 2026

Key points
  • Girls are exposed to greater scrutiny and judged more harshly on their appearance than boys.
  • Society favours beauty and sets "ideal" standards.
  • The “halo effect” suggests pretty people are assumed to possess other positive attributes.
Source: Free download from Pixabay/No-longer-here

My experience of being a girl and talking to hundreds of girls about their physical appearance tells me that we feel exposed to greater scrutiny, judged more harshly, and become more hung up on how we look than boys and men. But why?

Evolutionary theory suggests that the reason is in our DNA. The theory goes that males are attracted to females with a pretty face and an hourglass figure because these characteristics symbolise fertility and so these characteristics evolved. Females, meanwhile, are attracted to wealthy males who are physically strong because these traits show they can take care of us and our future offspring. The theory only accounts for heterosexual partner choice and doesn’t apply to independent women or those who choose not to reproduce.

Evidence from cross-cultural analysis of Lonely-Hearts columns in the 1990s showed that females tended to promote their physical beauty, whereas males emphasised material possessions and status.1 Internet dating profiles have been analysed in a similar way with similar findings, suggesting that the evolutionary theory still holds true.2

Feminist author Naomi Wolf explored what she called “women’s obsession” with physical perfection in her book The Beauty Myth.3 She argued that the pursuit of beauty entraps women and enslaves them to men. She coined the term “iron maiden” to describe an unrealistic and unreachable ideal, perpetuated by fashion and beauty industries, and used to punish women for failing to achieve and adhere to it.

But women and girls learn about “pretty privilege” long before we start dating or being interested in fashion. The term is relatively new, but the hypothesis that society favours beauty is not. In ancient fairy tales, beautiful girls are principled, clever and kind. They marry their prince and live happily ever after, while the ugly ones are stupid and evil and don’t. Psychologists call this the “halo effect”, whereby someone who is judged positively in one domain, such as beauty, is assumed to possess other positive attributes, such as compassion and competence. Research suggests that attractive women are more likely to be successful at job interviews, be promoted, earn more money and be more confident than those deemed less attractive.4

Fairy tales gave rise to the first Disney princess in 1937. Snow White was slim and pretty, with pink lips, brown eyes and skin as white as snow. Her eyes were later changed to blue, presumably because blue eyes on a girl were perceived as prettier than brown. Cinderella also had fair skin, blue eyes, pink lips and an hourglass figure. Ditto Sleeping Beauty. Ditto Ariel the Little Mermaid, who was slim, pretty and scantily clad. In 2023, the movie Barbie was said to explore feminism and patriarchy, yet advertisers bombarded us with yet more stereotypical, culturally biased images of what “pretty” should look like. Barbie the actress, Margot Robbie, just like those Disney princesses, is fair-skinned, blond-haired and blue-eyed with an hourglass figure.

So, what’s changed?

The reality is that women and girls still strive to squeeze – sometimes literally – into unrealistic and unreachable beauty “ideals”, which are now perpetuated by filtered online images and fuelled by “tweakments” and jabs. We know that “pretty” still bestows privilege, and that “body positivity”, the social movement that encouraged us to challenge prevailing standards and love our bodies no matter their shape and size, is the myth.

item.title: Menopause Might Not Drain Your Brain
item.description:
Menopause

Menopause Might Not Drain Your Brain

New research on all three female brain transitions changes the narrative.

Posted September 14, 2026

Source: Kaspars Eglitis / Unsplash

The story many women hear about menopause and the brain goes something like this: oestrogen declines, the brain changes, cognitive symptoms appear, and somehow the organ that has carried you through several decades is now beginning to fall apart.

The phrase “brain drain” captures the anxiety rather well.

There is some truth behind the concern: Women going through menopause commonly report problems with memory, concentration and other aspects of cognition, and previous research has found structural differences between pre- and post-menopausal brains. Menopause is a genuine period of neurological and hormonal change.

But a study published this week in Nature Communications suggests that we should think about one part of that story differently than we have.

Sophie van ’t Hof and colleagues at Amsterdam UMC compared brain structural changes across three major hormonal transitions: puberty, pregnancy and menopause. They used longitudinal MRI data and the same analytical approach across all three groups, with stable control groups included to help distinguish changes associated with the transitions themselves from the changes we would expect simply from normal development or ageing (van ’t Hof et al., 2026). In total, the study included 1,095 participants.

The puberty and pregnancy findings broadly followed what previous research has suggested: Girls going through menarche showed widespread reductions in cortical grey matter, as did women transitioning to motherhood. Some of the affected regions overlapped, particularly areas of the prefrontal, parietal and temporal cortex involved in higher-order cognitive functions.

Menopause looked very different. Women who went from being pre-menopausal at the first scan to post-menopausal at the second did not show a significant reduction in cortical or total grey matter volume. Meanwhile, women who remained pre-menopausal and women who remained post-menopausal during the same period showed the expected ongoing decline associated with ageing.

In other words, the women going through the menopausal transition did not show the accelerated volumetric loss you might expect from the “oestrogen disappears and the brain shrinks” narrative; if anything, the transition appeared to temporarily slow the decline.

This is where the study needs some careful handling. It would be very easy to turn these findings into a reassuring headline like “Menopause protects your brain!” That is not what the researchers found. The study looked specifically at structural brain volume. It does not tell us that menopause improves cognition or prevents Alzheimer's disease—or that the memory and concentration problems many women experience are somehow imagined.

What the researchers did find is that the structural trajectory during the transition from pre- to post-menopause was different from what they observed during puberty and pregnancy, and different from the ongoing changes seen in the stable control groups. They describe menopause as a “qualitatively distinct” pattern characterised by the absence rather than acceleration of volumetric change—and they do not yet know why (van ’t Hof et al., 2026).

The authors suggest that the pattern could reflect heightened plasticity or a temporary slowing of age-related decline, but the study cannot distinguish between those possibilities. They also describe the interpretation as preliminary.

One of the most interesting things about this study is that it puts three major hormonal transitions next to each other. Puberty, pregnancy and menopause all involve substantial changes in sex hormones. It would therefore be tempting to assume that the brain responds to all three in broadly the same way, but it doesn’t. Puberty and pregnancy produced broadly similar patterns of cortical grey matter reduction, although there were important differences between them; more than half of the cortical regions examined showed different patterns of change across the two transitions. Menopause was different again.

Scientifically, then, the statement, "The female brain responds to hormonal change,” is not particularly useful. Which hormonal change? At what point in life? Over what timescale? And what part of the brain? The brain is not a static organ waiting for hormones to tell it what to do. It is constantly adapting to changes in the body and environment, and different hormonal transitions can produce very different patterns of plasticity.

There is something almost counterintuitive about the menopause finding. The women who were going through menopause showed less volumetric decline than those who were not. But many women going through menopause also report that they feel cognitively different.

So what is happening? One possibility is that structural volume is simply not capturing the changes that matter for the symptoms women experience. Brain function, connectivity, neurotransmitter systems, blood flow and many other biological processes could change without producing an obvious reduction in grey matter volume.

For decades, research on women’s brains has had a fairly obvious problem: There simply wasn't enough of it. That gap has been particularly noticeable around hormonal transitions. Puberty, pregnancy and menopause are biologically enormous events, yet we have historically known much less about what happens to the brain during them than we should.

One longitudinal imaging study cannot tell us what menopause does to cognition, mental health or long-term dementia risk, but it does challenge the assumption that the menopausal transition should be understood primarily as a period of accelerated brain loss. The data do not support that interpretation but suggest that menopause has its own neurological trajectory, one that may temporarily attenuate the structural decline we normally associate with ageing.

item.title: Secure Attachment and Youth Loneliness
item.description:
Attachment

Secure Attachment and Youth Loneliness

The role of secure attachment in preventing loneliness and misuse of social media.

Posted September 14, 2026

Key points
  • Secure attachments are essential for cognitive, social, and emotional well-being.
  • Secure attachments prevent loneliness in young people by fostering bonding with others and social skills.
  • Research shows that secure attachments help prevent social media addiction and digital media misuse.
  • Parents can learn skills for establishing secure attachments in early life and throught the life cycle.

All the lonely people/Where do they all come from/All the lonely people/Where do they all belong

Lennon and McCartney

Source: pexels-cottonbro

With Gen Z now reporting the highest rates of loneliness of any generation, and parents more concerned than ever about the perils of social media amid recent suits against META, researchers and clinicians are increasingly pointing to something we’ve understood for decades: the power of a secure, trusting bond between a child and the adults who raise them.

In the psychological literature, they appear to be crucial for:

  • Effective and accurate cognitive functions
  • Emotional flexibility
  • Feeling safer and more secure
  • Finding meaning in experiences
  • Self-regulation and managing one’s own feelings and behaviors
  • The capacity for intimacy and healthy interpersonal relationships
  • Empathy
  • Self-awareness and comfort with one’s identity
  • Resilience

That’s a lot, and more than any parent or caregiver could possibly want for our kids, teens, and young adults. Kids with secure attachments tend to handle stress better, bounce back from setbacks, form closer friendships, and know themselves more clearly.

But how does this happen?

We humans are pack animals. We need each other. We need relationships.

As Winnicott so clearly pointed out, development requires both a biological endowment and a facilitating environment. The former is rooted in genetics and physical contributions to our development, and the second, perhaps most important part of our life experience, is rooted in relationships.

Dan Siegel summarized the process well. It is a gradual process, beginning and grounded in the first three years of life. Its components include:

  • Collaborative Communication: Parental attunement to the child
  • Reflective Dialogue: Creating the sense that subjective experience is important and can be shared. This allows the child to be seen
  • Repair: Identification and repair of miscommunications and misunderstandings. This requires that both parent and child are mindful of breaches, and use apology and reparations, to mend fences
  • Emotional Communication: Sharing and amplifying the positive and mitigating the negative in the interpersonal world of parent and child
  • Developing Coherent Narratives: Helping the child and teen develop an internal autobiographical sense of self, and self-awareness, key for self-reflection and a solid sense of identity

Attachment theory has shaped how we understand social and emotional development, parenting, and our own relational patterns. Yet little research addresses how secure attachment protects against specific, longstanding threats to youth development.

In particular, let’s consider loneliness and misuse of social media.

Secure Attachment and Loneliness

On May 3, 2023, The United States Surgeon General Dr. Vivek Murthy released a new Advisory calling attention to the public health crisis of loneliness, isolation, and lack of connection in our country.

According to the Advisory, social connection is a critical but underappreciated contributor to individual overall health, community safety, and resilience. Yet, around half of all U.S. adults report experiencing loneliness, with some of the highest rates among our young people. In fact, today the Gen Z population reports the highest rates of loneliness.

The Surgeon General noted that it is important to “Invest in your relationship with your child or loved one by recognizing that strong, secure attachments are protective and a good foundation for other healthy relationships.”

The report didn’t specify how to foster these attachments (practical examples follow below.) There have been some studies (though few) on how secure attachment mitigates loneliness.

Consider a teenager who gets left out of a group chat, or shows up to find plans have changed without them. A securely attached teen is more likely to mention it to a parent that night, or reach out to another friend, rather than sitting with it alone and assuming the worst about themselves.

Teenagers’ needs for bonding with others, feeling fulfilled, and trust are grounded in their secure attachment profile. As such, they are more likely to seek help and support when distressed, rather than worrying alone. Their sense of connection to others also helps them build highly developed social skills, mitigating temporary isolation without it developing into chronic loneliness. Their sense of connection becomes a part of their autobiographical narrative, and is an important outcome of secure attachment.

Secure Attachment and Problematic Social Media Use

Parents, caregivers, clinicians, and legislators alike have grown concerned about digital media because of both its habit-forming design, and the way young people can misuse it, for instance, for bullying, excessive texting, or ghosting.

Though research is limited, evidence suggests that secure attachments reduce vulnerability to digital media misuse. One study linked insecure attachment to social media addiction, with social support outside of media use acting as a mediator. Another study found secure attachment associated with less addiction and fewer mental health problems.

Secure attachments can reduce a young person’s need to look to social media for validation, emotional regulation, and relief from negative emotions.

None of this means social media is inherently harmful—for many young people, it’s a genuine source of connection and community. The point is more specific: When a young person already feels secure and connected, they’re less likely to depend on a device to meet needs the device can’t fulfill.

What Can Parents and Caregivers Do

With Siegel’s framework in mind, here are some guidelines for nurturing secure attachment:

  • When your child is upset, slow down, get on their level, name their feelings, and match your tone before jumping to solutions.
  • Ask an open question about their day, and sit with the whole answer with curiosity, instead of moving straight to advice.
  • After a blowup, come back later and name what happened. You might say, “I got too frustrated earlier, and I’m sorry” or something similar. The repair matters more than the rupture.
  • Identify and name positive moments aloud in the moment they happen so the good moments register. This could look like, “I love that we laughed about that together,” or “I enjoyed watching that with you.”
  • To facilitate narrative building skills, ask your teen to tell you about their day as a story instead of a checklist. For example, try phrases like, “Walk me through your day,” as opposed to “How was school.”

Promoting secure attachments is not easy. For many, Siegel’s skills are complicated by real obstacles: parents’ own insecure attachment histories; adverse childhood experiences; economic pressure; disparities related to race, immigration status, or gender identity; unstable family structure; domestic conflict; or psychiatric or physical disability.

It is imperative to recognize these obstacles and seek support — from family, friends, spiritual leaders, or mental health professionals.

And in the process of getting help, parents and caregivers may not only promote secure attachments with their children but earn secure attachment profiles for themselves.
